title: CPO Test Won't Scale Without Standardization
gist: Co-packaged optics is ramping into AI data centers, but every CPO design today requires a custom test cell — no standards exist for fiber connectors, product specs, or test data formats — which caps throughput and keeps cost of test high. Multiple industry participants (Intel Foundry, Amkor, Teradyne, Advantest, Lightmatter, Ayar Labs) argue profitability arrives only with standardization, and the least-discussed blocker is a data problem: STDF cannot carry optical measurements as first-class objects, so cross-vendor yield learning degrades into manual reconciliation.

themes.theme: Why CPO is displacing pluggables now

insights.claim: Scale-up interconnect carries roughly 10x the bandwidth requirement of scale-out, which is the specific reason traditional pluggable optics fail and optics must move onto the package next to the GPU.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale-up/scale-out split that determines which optics vendors get designed into AI racks; pluggable-optics revenue is structurally exposed on the scale-up side.
insights.quote: Scale-up has about 10X the bandwidth requirement of scale-out, and so traditional pluggables don’t work.
insights.locator: Traditionally, optics have been done with pluggables

insights.claim: Optics integration is following a two-step path: near-package optics on the board reaching volume production in 12 to 18 months, followed by co-packaged optics on the substrate reaching volume in 18 to 24 months.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A datable roadmap for when optical content actually hits volume revenue — useful for timing exposure to photonics suppliers and test equipment makers.
insights.quote: The first step would be an NPO (near package optics), which brings the optical into the board, which is not in volume production yet. I expect that to get into volume production in 12 to 18 months’ time.
insights.locator: The industry is taking a stepwise approach to optics integration

insights.claim: Nvidia and Broadcom have already introduced CPO solutions and are heavily ramping them into volume, while the broader ecosystem is still in a proof-of-concept phase working to reduce assembly time.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: The two largest networking-silicon players are ahead of the standards process, meaning their choices will set the de facto interfaces others must match.
insights.quote: Nvidia and Broadcom have introduced those solutions, and they are heavily ramping this into volume right now.
insights.locator: The industry is taking a stepwise approach to optics integration

insights.claim: The proliferation of options for heterogeneous integration, thermal management, serviceability, and manufacturing test is itself slowing CPO rollout — the constraint is choice overload, not technical feasibility.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Reframes CPO risk: bottleneck is ecosystem fragmentation and test cost, not physics — so watch consolidation of designs, not lab breakthroughs, as the ramp signal.
insights.locator: CPO checks all the boxes for next-gen computing

insights.claim: Some CPO architectures deliberately keep the laser external to the package because the laser is the highest-risk component from a reliability perspective, a tradeoff made against thermals, manufacturability, yield, and field replaceability.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: External-laser architectures create a separate serviceable component market and change which supplier owns the reliability risk in an AI rack.
insights.quote: For instance, one example of CPO is to have external lasers because the laser is the high-risk part from a reliability perspective.
insights.locator: Many of the priorities here are shared with mainstream semiconductor assembly

themes.theme: Custom test cells as the cost bottleneck

insights.claim: There are currently no standards for CPO connectors, product specifications, or test data formats, so every CPO design requires a custom test solution — producing longer time to market, higher cost, and limited reuse of equipment and software.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Cost of test is the hidden gross-margin drag on CPO products today; the first vendors to standardize capture the economics of reuse.
insights.locator: Nearly every aspect of the physical test cell poses a challenge

insights.claim: Current CPO designs integrate anywhere from 4 to 36 optical engines across two to four sides of a compute die, with no common approach to fiber connectors, alignment schemes, or laser delivery.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A 9x spread in optical engine count per package means test-cell hardware cannot be amortized — the concrete measure of fragmentation blocking automation.
insights.quote: Current designs integrate anywhere from 4 to 36 optical engines across two to four sides of a compute die, and the industry still lacks a common approach to fiber connectors, alignment schemes, and laser delivery.
insights.locator: Today, CPO packages vary widely from test program to test program

insights.claim: Connector standardization is a gating item because manufacturing test may require tens of thousands of insertions over a connector's lifecycle, and a connector design that cannot survive that cannot be used in production.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Insertion-count durability is a concrete qualification hurdle that will eliminate connector designs — a screening criterion for optical connector suppliers.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, a handful of assertions is needed over the connector’s lifecycle

insights.claim: Standardization is framed as removing unnecessary variation in how co-packaged optics are accessed, stimulated, measured, and reported — creating common expectations around test access, reference conditions, terminology, calibration practice, and result reporting.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A concrete five-part checklist for judging whether any proposed CPO standard actually reduces cost, versus standards theater.
insights.locator: Standards can help the industry by reducing unnecessary variation

insights.claim: Standardization would let each ecosystem layer specialize: suppliers building equipment to a specific performance envelope, customers architecting products to defined data rates and failure-rate specs, and OSATs defining production test cells with pre-defined success criteria.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Describes the value-chain reorganization CPO standardization would trigger — each tier's margin depends on which layer captures the standard.
insights.locator: Standards are expected to play a vital role

insights.claim: A comprehensive list of fabrication defect types in silicon-optical structures is being compiled from about half a dozen fab houses, and that data is expected to set test priority and test limits for the industry.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Defect-driven test limits are the precondition for cutting redundant test content — an early, concrete step toward lower CPO cost of test.
insights.locator: A comprehensive list of fabrication defect types

insights.claim: OSAT success depends on deploying test equipment that spans a wide product range — including optical engines and switches operating in both the O-band and C-band — specifically to maximize CapEx reuse.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: CapEx reuse is the OSAT profitability lever in CPO; equipment vendors selling narrow single-band testers will struggle to win OSAT budget.
insights.quote: This will allow for maximum CapEx re-use.
insights.locator: For instance, customers have optical engines and optical switches

themes.theme: De facto standards outrunning standards bodies

insights.claim: The CPO market is evolving faster than traditional standards bodies can respond, so industry leaders are setting de facto standards through their own market adoption, consortia, and multi-source agreements.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Bet on the lead-customer choices rather than formal standards processes when picking CPO winners; MSA participation is the tell.
insights.quote: The challenge is that the CPO market is evolving faster than traditional standards bodies can typically respond,
insights.locator: When to implement standards has always included an element of guesswork

insights.claim: Optical connectivity is already beginning to converge based on the evaluation and deployment decisions of leading customers and system providers, not formal industry standards.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Connector convergence is happening now via buyer power — a near-term catalyst that would unlock test automation and cut CPO cost.
insights.locator: In some areas, such as optical connectivity

insights.claim: Lightmatter has partnered with other Open Compute Project members on an open rack-level reference design whose specifications and standardization are intended to let the ecosystem scale to 10 million CPO units per year, with test specifications included.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: 10 million units/year is the stated scale target — the yardstick against which current custom-test-cell throughput must be judged.
insights.locator: Standards

insights.claim: Equipment vendors and OSATs generally follow their lead customers rather than driving standards themselves, meaning standardization will be pulled by a small number of large buyers.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Watch hyperscaler and lead-GPU-vendor procurement specs as the real standards documents; supplier roadmaps are downstream of them.
insights.quote: several of them also noted that equipment vendors and OSATs often follow their lead customers.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: The least-appreciated CPO scaling obstacle is a data problem rather than a hardware one, because STDF was built for electrical parametric and functional results and cannot carry a wavelength sweep or polarization-dependent loss curve as a first-class object.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, fixable software-standard gap that gates CPO yield learning — an underpriced problem relative to the attention on packaging hardware.
insights.quote: STDF was built for electrical parametric and functional results. It was never designed to carry a wavelength sweep or a polarization-dependent loss curve as a first-class object.
insights.locator: However, the chip industry has yet to settle on a data model

insights.claim: Because there is no optical data model, optical measurements get flattened into scalar limits or parked in vendor-specific files, destroying the richness needed for yield learning before analysis even begins.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Data loss at the format layer means CPO yield ramps will be slower than electrical-only precedents suggest — a schedule risk for optical-heavy roadmaps.
insights.locator: However, the chip industry has yet to settle on a data model

insights.claim: Because STDF cannot represent wavelength sweeps, far-field profiles, OSA traces, or LIV curves, every vendor invents its own format, and an STDF extension or equally disciplined parallel format would accelerate downstream analytics.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A named, concrete standards deliverable to track; its arrival would be a leading indicator that CPO test cost is about to fall.
insights.quote: STDF was never really designed with optical measurements in mind — wavelength sweeps, far-field profiles, OSA traces, LIV curves — so every vendor invents something,
insights.locator: Others also point to the need for test data format standardization

insights.claim: Most CPO standardization effort has gone to physical and electrical interfaces while test-data standardization is neglected, yet interoperable modules are worthless for yield learning if each supplier reports optical parameters in a different schema.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Points to where standardization would most directly reduce cost of test — a mispriced priority relative to where industry attention currently sits.
insights.locator: Most of the standardization efforts so far have focused on physical and electrical interfaces

insights.claim: Three specific data gaps must close for CPO analytics: universal optical test output formats across ATE providers, uniform die identification protocols among PIC and EIC vendors with defined OSAT ID handling, and standardized test metadata for environmental conditions, recipe versions, and hardware status.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A concrete three-item scorecard for assessing whether any CPO analytics claim is real or bespoke integration work in disguise.
insights.locator: Meg O’Brien, director of product engineering at Lightmatter, highlighted three areas

insights.claim: CPO traceability requires a readable physical or virtual ID on every component in final assembly — EICs, PICs, lasers, fiber connectors, splitters, combiners, substrates, and heatsinks — plus a data platform that stitches those IDs together.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Defines the minimum viable traceability architecture; suppliers lacking component-level IDs become the weak link that blocks a customer's yield program.
insights.locator: Traceability

insights.claim: IDs are easily dropped in transfers between factories, and the fix is contractual rather than technical — writing ID-propagation requirements directly into OSAT statements of work and verifying them at incoming inspection.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Actionable diligence question for anyone evaluating a CPO manufacturer: does the OSAT contract mandate ID propagation, or is yield learning structurally impossible?
insights.quote: It’s a contract problem. Anyone serious about CPO yield learning needs to write ID-propagation requirements directly into their OSAT statements of work and check them at incoming.
insights.locator: But IDs are easily dropped during the transfer from one factory to the next

insights.claim: Analytics platforms cannot recover traceability data that was never captured on the factory floor, so the failure is upstream of any software tool.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Deflates claims that an analytics purchase solves CPO yield learning; the spend must go to factory data capture first.
insights.quote: But we can’t manufacture data that nobody captured.
insights.locator: This isn’t a technology problem

insights.claim: Traceability must preserve identity, lot history, test conditions, calibration state, and performance results across the supply chain without exposing any supplier's proprietary process details — an explicit IP-boundary design constraint.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: The IP-protection requirement is why a neutral data layer, not a vertically integrated one, is the likely winning architecture in multi-supplier CPO flows.
insights.locator: Others agree that with traceability comes the acknowledgment

insights.claim: Tracking a single CPO module's lifecycle spans EIC and PIC dies, laser components, final assembly, every test insertion, and potential rework cycles — making traceability primarily a data-modeling problem.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Rework loops in the genealogy are what break naive traceability schemes; a practical test of whether a vendor's platform is production-grade.
insights.locator: Supporting traceability in a CPO environment is primarily a challenge of data modeling

insights.claim: Electrical and optical test results live in fundamentally different data worlds — parametric bins and pass/fail on one side, spectral sweeps, insertion loss, return loss, wavelength and polarization on the other — and yield learning only occurs when both can be correlated on the same physical unit.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Cross-flow correlation capability is the differentiator among yield-analytics vendors chasing the CPO market.
insights.quote: CPO test is where data analytics stops being optional,
insights.locator: Yield learning and more

insights.claim: Teams moving fastest on CPO treat multi-domain correlation as a first-class capability rather than a post-mortem activity, enabling questions like whether an optical margin loss tracks a specific bond process, EIC lot, or test site.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: An operational tell for separating CPO leaders from laggards during diligence: is correlation built into the flow or bolted on after failures?
insights.locator: The teams moving fastest on CPO

insights.claim: In photonic manufacturing flows resembling CPO, analytics value lands in three consistent places: merging all data streams onto one canvas, unit-level commonality and outlier screening such as PAT and MV-PAT, and giving executives, process owners and the test team a single shared report.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Concrete ROI taxonomy for CPO analytics spend, drawn from existing photonics flows rather than projection.
insights.locator: We’ve worked with photonic manufacturers running flows

insights.claim: Correlating bar-test electricals with far-field optical metrics surfaces relationships invisible in isolation — for example, units with marginal threshold current being the ones that lose far-field power two insertions later.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: A worked example of the predictive screening CPO makers forgo without correlated data — real scrap avoided per unit.
insights.quote: Units with marginal threshold current are the ones losing far-field power two insertions later.
insights.locator: If you can correlate bar-test electricals with far-field optical metrics

insights.claim: The binding difficulty in CPO yield analytics is data merging, not the statistical methods themselves.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Value accrues to data-plumbing and traceability vendors rather than algorithm vendors in the CPO analytics stack.
insights.quote: The hard part is almost never the math. It’s getting the data merged in the first place.
insights.locator: Third is having executives, process owners, and the test team

insights.claim: Improving CPO yield requires expertise spanning EIC and PIC fabrication, assembly, and both optical and system-level testing — a breadth rarely found within a single engineering discipline, which is why a centralized data platform is used to bridge the silos.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Organizational capability, not equipment, is the scarce input in CPO yield ramps — a barrier favoring vertically capable players like Lightmatter and Intel Foundry.
insights.locator: Improving yield for co-packaged photonics necessitates expertise

insights.claim: The stated bottom line is that CPO test will not scale if every product, supplier, package, optical interface, and test cell is treated as a custom engineering project; interoperability at the boundaries is the goal, not disclosure of proprietary design or process detail.
insights.speaker: Anne Meixner
insights.so_what: Sets the pass/fail condition for CPO reaching 10M units/year — a milestone with direct read-through to AI networking capacity and optics supplier revenue.
insights.quote: CPO test will not scale if every product, supplier, package, optical interface, and test cell is treated as a custom engineering project.
insights.locator: Conclusion
